text: The network from Lessons 6 and 7 looks correct on paper — subnets sized right, NSG and security group rules scoped to specific sources and ports. Looking correct and being correct aren't the same thing, and this lesson covers the cheap way to close that gap: verifying connectivity before anything real gets deployed on top of it.

Deploy one small, disposable VM or EC2 instance into each tier, using the real NSG or security group from Lesson 7 rather than a theoretical reading of the rules. az vm create with the actual vnet, subnet, and nsg, or the AWS equivalent run-instances with the real subnet and security group, puts the rules under an actual test instead of just a code review.

Real verification checks both directions, not just whether something can be reached. From the web test VM, confirm it can reach the internet on port 443, and confirm it cannot reach the data tier's database port. From the app test VM, confirm it can reach the database port but cannot be reached directly from the internet. Simple tools like ping, Test-NetConnection, or nc handle the basic checks; Azure Network Watcher and AWS Reachability Analyzer trace a specific path through the rules and report exactly which one allowed or blocked it.

If the data tier turns out to be reachable from the internet, catching it here costs a few minutes: edit the rule, redeploy the test VM, verify again, and nothing else was ever exposed to begin with. Catching the same misconfiguration after Chapter 3's real compute and real data are already deployed on top of it means the fix is still the same one-line edit, but now there's an incident write-up attached to it, not just a quick correction.

The network layer for this chapter is done and verified in both directions. Chapter 3 picks up from here, deploying the real VMs and EC2 instances into the subnets this chapter built, secured, and proved out before anything else was allowed to touch them.
